text: The 2007 development agreement doesn't discuss a no-rise certification in the development agreement, but I don't think it has to.

speaker: brianquinn
text: I thought you just told Justice Doss that it did address it. I guess I'm a little confused now.

speaker: daniellehatchit
text: I apologize, Your Honor. The Unified Development Code back in 2004 discusses the no-rise certification requirement.

speaker: brianquinn
text: So the 2007 agreement didn't?

speaker: daniellehatchit
text: Correct. The 2007 development agreement, drainage easement agreement, the permits don't discuss that. They instead just discuss what drainage improvement requirements are going to be required for the project, and they say they're going to be on the city.

speaker: brianquinn
text: And your argument that somehow the no-rise was dispensed with in 2007 via the development agreements?

speaker: daniellehatchit
text: Yes, Your Honor, because what is required for a no-rise certification is basically to bring water off your property. And what the development agreements provided for, again, is that the easement would be used to convey surface water from our property, and that the city would pay for that, and that they would continue to make improvements to that.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Thank you, Counsel. Your time's expired. Justice Park, do you have any questions?

speaker: daniellehatchit
text: No questions.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Justice Doss, any questions? Nothing else. Thanks. Thank you, Ms. Hatchett.

speaker: daniellehatchit
text: Thank you, Your Honor.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Five minutes, Mr. High.

speaker: georgehyde
text: Thank you, Your Honor. May it please the Court. First of all, I will, that you do need to adjudicate whether 245 applies in this case, because an exception to 245 in the subsection 3 has to do with areas that are covered as a floodplain, and the area where this easement is is part of improvements in a FEMA-dedicated floodplain, and we've asserted that exception to any allegation of vested rights relating to drainage, because that's what the provision applies. And when opposing counsels, and again, the city was willing to believe, or the city wants you to think with regards to the limitation of 245 to land-use regulations, it's the city quoting the statute. It's the actual words in the statute that specifically say land-use regulation is the only thing that you get vested in. Now, development agreements, as I've mentioned before, have a number of different provisions that can go in them, including anything that's lawful that the people feel is appropriate. I'm stating that because everything in a development agreement is not a land-use development regulation. But, as in this one, there are some land-use regulations that are in the development agreement. For instance, the setbacks requirements for buildings and so forth is in the development agreement that says that if we change the setbacks, they get to use the setbacks that were in place in 2007. There are provisions in there for water and wastewater delivery, which we exchanged this. One of the reasons why development agreements come in is that people want to, outside of the city limits, they want to hook up for water and wastewater services, and that was part of this deal, too. There were three things regarding impervious cover and other things that had to be done to certain lots within the property in order to hook up to water and wastewater.

speaker: brianquinn
text: So those regulations— Council, do you agree or disagree that the City of Buda received an easement? I agree. And what was—OK, received an easement. What was the consideration for the easement? It was a negotiated easement, I guess.

speaker: georgehyde
text: The negotiated easement provided for the water and wastewater services and to manage and control the—I need my glasses—the various land use outside in the ETJ. So it's a written contract. We guaranteed the continuation of the extraterritorial jurisdiction.

speaker: brianquinn
text: OK, but the consideration for the easement was what? The city was supposed to take care of the costs for doing that drainage?

speaker: georgehyde
text: The city was to build a drainage easement.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Was to build a drainage easement.

speaker: georgehyde
text: I'm sorry, a drainage way in the easement.

speaker: brianquinn
text: OK. And it did that. And they did that. And your argument is that does not encompass any no-rise issues.

speaker: georgehyde
text: That's correct. And when you look at the agreement, it discusses how—that the property needed fill. And in order to—and they said everything you dig out of the easement, you can put it there to help us get up and get closer to above the floodplain. But there's no obligations whatsoever that say that we are required to place fill in the property in order to get it above the floodplain.

speaker: brianquinn
text: In order to resolve this jurisdictional dispute, in your view, do we have to adjudicate the meaning or the scope of what was encompassed within the consideration given for the easement? Whether or not the drainage issue includes no-rise or not.

speaker: georgehyde
text: I think that that's an issue that may be disputed in the case because—

speaker: brianquinn
text: I understand, but do we need to adjudicate— do we need to interpret the agreement with regard to the easement and the consideration and what the parties agreed to back then in order to determine whether or not there's jurisdiction now?

speaker: georgehyde
text: Yes, I think you do. I think if you look at it and you say that there was an obligation of the city to develop it to no-rise— and actually, it matters on how you take the 245 exception because if you apply the exception that goes to floodplains, which is what we've asserted, then it doesn't matter because then they don't have vested rights, period. But if you say that the exception doesn't apply, then you would have to determine whether or not there's some type of damage to the remainder of the property by virtue of their exaction claims or their investment-backed expectations for no-rise.

speaker: larrydoss
text: And you're saying the no-rise certification falls under the federal exception?

speaker: georgehyde
text: No, I'm saying that Chapter 245 has an exception— I think it's like subsection 4 or 5— to drainage facilities that are within a FEMA-designated floodplain. And these facilities are within a FEMA-designated floodplain, and therefore, Chapter 245 does not apply to these drainage facilities because they're specifically accepted by the exceptions in 245.

speaker: brianquinn
text: And that's undisputed, that they are within the FEMA—

speaker: georgehyde
text: Yes, Your Honor.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Whatever.

speaker: georgehyde
text: Yeah, I mean, that's really the whole thing, is that three-quarters of the property is in the floodplain and they've got to lift it up out of the floodplain to develop it.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Thank you, counsel. Your time has expired. We appreciate it. Justice Clark, do you have any questions?

speaker: daniellehatchit
text: No questions.

speaker: brianquinn
text: Justice Dawson? I don't have anything. Counsel, we appreciate you appearing in front of us via Zoom. Hopefully, there will be a time in the near future where we can have these arguments in person, and I know I'm hoping for that time. But with that said, your case is submitted and you are excused.
